title: Challenge bonus-d: Notifications
description: Notification hygiene, mentions, subscriptions, and avoiding overload.
concepts: Notification hygiene, mentions, subscriptions, and avoiding overload.
transcriptText:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're talking about GitHub notifications, which sounds small until your inbox starts shouting at you from six directions at once.

[JAMIE]
And that is exactly when people either miss something important, like a review request, or they give up and ignore everything.

[ALEX]
Exactly. So the goal here is not to get more notifications. It's to build a notification system that keeps you informed about what matters and filters out noise.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
GitHub notifications are how GitHub tells you that something may need your attention. That might be a mention, a review request, an assignment, activity on a thread you joined, a failing CI check on your pull request, or sometimes a release from a repository you watch closely.

[JAMIE]
So this is really about attention management.

[ALEX]
Yes. And for this workshop, this part is guided practice, not an automated check. Notification settings are account-level, so the Learning Room bot can't validate them for you. Instead, you practice configuring, filtering, and acting.

[JAMIE]
That matters because learners sometimes think, if a bot isn't checking it, maybe it's optional.

[ALEX]
Not optional. Just not auto-graded. The evidence here is a structured completion comment on your assigned challenge issue.

[JAMIE]
And the practical goal is a useful workflow: set a watch level, use filters, and perform at least one inbox action.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let's anchor this in the guided walkthrough. The recommended practice is simple.
Open your Learning Room repository on GitHub.com. Find the Watch button near the top right, close to Star and Fork. Open that menu and set the repository to Participating and @mentions.

[JAMIE]
Why that choice?

[ALEX]
Because it's usually the sweet spot. You'll hear about conversations that directly involve you without getting every single issue and comment from the whole repository.

[JAMIE]
Then you go to the notifications inbox.

[ALEX]
Right. You can browse to github dot com slash notifications, or use the bell in the GitHub header. If you use GitHub keyboard shortcuts, you can press G, then N. Sequentially, not at the same time.

[JAMIE]
That sequence detail matters, especially for screen reader users.

[ALEX]
It does. In browse mode, press G, release it, then press N.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Once you're in the inbox, practice using filters. First try Review requested. That shows notifications where someone asked you to review a pull request. Then clear it and try Assigned, which shows issues and pull requests assigned to you.

[JAMIE]
So the lesson is not just, here is a big list. It's, learn to shrink the list to the kind of work you need right now.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Then open one notification, read it briefly, go back, and perform one inbox action on a non-critical thread. Either mute it or mark it done.

[JAMIE]
Let's define those carefully because they sound similar.

[ALEX]
Good instinct. Mark done removes the item from your inbox for now, but future activity can bring it back if it still involves you. Mute is stronger. It tells GitHub you do not want future updates from that thread.

[JAMIE]
So mark done is more like, I handled this for now. Mute is, please stop notifying me about this conversation.

[ALEX]
Perfectly said.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
If you're completing the workshop evidence, your completion comment should state three things: the watch level you set, the filters you tested, and the inbox action you performed.

[JAMIE]
Such as: watch level set to Participating and @mentions, filters tested Review requested and Assigned, inbox action performed mute on some thread.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And then close your Chapter 10 challenge issue.

[JAMIE]
What are the expected outcomes here?

[ALEX]
You should be able to configure repository watch levels to reduce noise, find review requests and assigned work quickly using filters, and reduce notification overload with mute or done.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's talk about getting stuck, because notifications can be weirdly slippery.

[ALEX]
Yes. Common problems include not finding the Watch button, having an empty inbox, shortcuts not working, or filters showing nothing.

[JAMIE]
If someone can't find Watch?

[ALEX]
Look near the top right of the repository page, in the same row as Star and Fork.

[JAMIE]
If the inbox is empty?

[ALEX]
That's okay. You may not have any new notifications yet. Switch to the Done tab and practice there on an older notification.

[JAMIE]
If keyboard shortcuts like M or E don't work?

[ALEX]
Your screen reader may be intercepting them. Click or otherwise focus the notification row first, then try the shortcut.

[JAMIE]
And if filters appear broken?

[ALEX]
Clear all active filters first, then apply one at a time.

[JAMIE]
I also like the human fallback.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. Ask a facilitator to model one inbox action live, then repeat it yourself.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now let's step back and answer the basic question: what generates a notification?

[JAMIE]
Because once you understand the causes, the inbox makes more sense.

[ALEX]
You get notifications when someone @mentions your username in an issue, pull request, or discussion. You get them when a pull request is assigned to you for review. You get them when an issue or PR is assigned to you. You also get them when there's activity on a thread you're subscribed to, which can happen because you commented, were mentioned, or chose to subscribe. A CI or Actions failure on your PR can generate a notification. And if you are watching a repository broadly enough, a published release can also notify you.

[JAMIE]
So GitHub is combining direct involvement, explicit assignment, and repository-level subscriptions.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And that is why notification management matters. If you subscribe too broadly, the signal gets buried.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's unpack subscription levels, because this is where many learners accidentally create chaos.

[ALEX]
For each repository, you choose how much you want to hear.
Participating and @mentions means only conversations where you participated, were assigned, or were mentioned.
All Activity means every issue, every comment, every pull request, every update.
Ignore means no notifications from that repository at all.
Custom gives you finer control, such as issues only, pull requests only, or releases.

[JAMIE]
And the recommendation for most repositories in this workshop is Participating and @mentions.

[ALEX]
Yes. It keeps you in the loop without flooding you.

[JAMIE]
How does a blind or low-vision learner change that setting accessibly?

[ALEX]
On a repository page, find the Watch button in the header. On Windows with NVDA or JAWS, button navigation can help you reach it. Press Enter to open the dropdown, use arrow keys to move through the options, then press Enter to select one. The button label updates to confirm your choice.

[JAMIE]
And on macOS with VoiceOver?

[ALEX]
Use Quick Nav or standard VoiceOver navigation to find the Watch or Unwatch button, activate it with VO+Space, move through the options with VO navigation or arrows, and select with VO+Space. Again, listen for the updated button label.

[JAMIE]
That confirmation matters. You want proof the change stuck.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let's move into the notifications inbox itself. On GitHub.com, the browser is the main place to manage notifications. You can open the inbox at github dot com slash notifications. Once there, keyboard shortcuts are useful: E to mark done, I to toggle read or unread, and Shift+M to mute a thread.

[JAMIE]
And there was also a shorter mention of M for mute in the guided challenge.

[ALEX]
Right. The important learning point is that GitHub provides keyboard-driven inbox actions, but exact behavior and shortcuts can evolve. The web interface is the authoritative place for full inbox management.

[JAMIE]
What about VS Code?

[ALEX]
If you use the GitHub Pull Requests extension, there is a Notifications view in the GitHub sidebar that can surface items needing attention. You can open a related issue or pull request directly in VS Code.

[JAMIE]
And GitHub Desktop?

[ALEX]
GitHub Desktop does not manage notifications. Use the browser or CLI for that.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Speaking of CLI, there were some command-line examples here.

[ALEX]
Yes, and they're practical. If you want to list pull requests requesting your review, a very common type of notification, you can run a GitHub CLI search for open PRs review-requested from you. To open the notifications page in your browser, you can use gh browse notifications.

[JAMIE]
And there were also examples using the API.

[ALEX]
Right. You can query notifications with gh api, list open issues assigned to you with gh issue list, and inspect a specific PR with gh pr view. But there is an important limitation: the GitHub CLI does not have a full first-class notifications command for all inbox management. For actions like mark as read, mute, or archive-style workflows, the web inbox is still the main interface.

[JAMIE]
So CLI is great for checking status and finding work, but not the complete replacement.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now, what is the notifications page like structurally? Think of it as a list of notification items, each usually exposed as a link or row you can open. A notification typically announces its title, the repository it belongs to, and the reason you received it, such as mention, review request, or assignment.

[JAMIE]
That means screen reader users should expect repeated patterns.

[ALEX]
Yes. The list is a strength once you recognize the pattern. Move through notifications item by item, listen for title, repository, and reason, then decide whether to open, mark done, mute, or leave it for later.

[JAMIE]
That sounds much more manageable than hearing it as an undifferentiated wall of links.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Pattern recognition reduces cognitive load.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's do the common tasks people actually need.

[ALEX]
A very common one is finding pull requests that need your review. In the web inbox, use the Review requested filter. In the CLI, search for PRs with review requested from you.

[JAMIE]
Another common one is checking assigned work.

[ALEX]
Use the Assigned filter in the inbox, or list issues assigned to you from the CLI. Both give you a focused queue.

[JAMIE]
And if you open a specific notification and want to understand the PR status?

[ALEX]
Open the notification's title link and inspect the pull request page. In CLI workflows, you can use gh pr view with the PR number and repository.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Filtering is the real superpower here. You can filter the inbox by reason, like review requests or assignments. You can also filter by repository or organization.

[JAMIE]
Why is filtering by repository or organization useful?

[ALEX]
Because sometimes the noise isn't personal, it's contextual. Maybe you only want to see notifications from the workshop organization, or from one active repository, instead of mixing them with everything else in your GitHub life.

[JAMIE]
So if someone uses multiple repositories, teams, or identities, filters become part of the daily routine.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Instead of reading every item in arrival order, you ask: what kind of work am I checking right now?

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's talk about scale. What happens when there are too many notifications?

[ALEX]
Then you need strategy, not heroics. One approach is the mark-all-as-done workflow, used carefully. That means acknowledging that you do not need to preserve every old item in the active inbox. Clear the backlog once you've decided nothing critical is hiding there, then rely on targeted filters and direct notifications going forward.

[JAMIE]
Used carefully is doing a lot of work in that sentence.

[ALEX]
Yes. Don't blindly wipe out the inbox if you're unsure. Scan for review requests, assignments, and mentions first.

[JAMIE]
What about a noisy thread?

[ALEX]
Mute it. If one issue or PR keeps generating updates you no longer need, muting is appropriate. It's especially useful when a discussion balloons after your part is done.

[JAMIE]
And how about the uncomfortable case: you got @mentioned and didn't expect it.

[ALEX]
First, figure out whether action is actually required. Sometimes a mention is informational. If it does not need you, you might mark it done after reading, or mute the thread if it will stay noisy. The key is not to let every mention hijack your attention equally.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now we should discuss account-level notification settings, because repository watch settings are only part of the picture.

[JAMIE]
This is the bonus mastery piece.

[ALEX]
Yes. At github dot com slash settings slash notifications, you can configure how GitHub contacts you. The reference setup contrasts defaults with a more intentional configuration.

[JAMIE]
Start with the default problem.

[ALEX]
With default settings, GitHub may send email notifications for every issue and pull request in every repository you watch, every comment on threads you've participated in, and every CI status update. That becomes overwhelming fast. Many people end up ignoring all GitHub email, which defeats the purpose.

[JAMIE]
So the reference solution is not saying all defaults are bad. It's saying defaults often create too much volume.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
A more productive setup looks like this.
For Participating notifications, email on and web on. If someone replies where you're actively involved, you usually want to know.
For Watching notifications, email off and web on. That means watched repository activity is available in GitHub when you choose to check it, but it does not constantly interrupt your email.
For GitHub Actions, email off for successful runs and on for failed runs only.

[JAMIE]
That last one is elegant. A passing check usually doesn't require action.

[ALEX]
Exactly. A green check on the PR page is enough. Failures are what need attention.

[JAMIE]
And repository-level watching?

[ALEX]
For repositories where you actively contribute, watching all activity can make sense. For repositories you read occasionally, use Custom, often issues and pull requests only. For repositories you've finished with, unwatch them.

[JAMIE]
That last one may be the most life-changing.

[ALEX]
It often is. Old subscriptions quietly clog your feed.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What if someone uses multiple email addresses?

[ALEX]
Then custom routing can help. For example, route workshop or Community-Access organization notifications to your workshop email, and send personal project notifications to your personal email.

[JAMIE]
So the inbox structure can reflect the role you're playing.

[ALEX]
Yes. That separation can reduce confusion and help you maintain boundaries.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Can you explain the reasoning behind these settings one more time in plain language?

[ALEX]
Certainly. Email off for watching reduces constant interruption from low-priority updates. You can still check the GitHub notification bell or the web inbox when you are ready. Actions failures only keeps your attention on breakage, not routine success. Unwatching finished repositories keeps your inbox relevant to current work.

[JAMIE]
So the principle is deliberate signal selection.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Intentional notification management.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
There's also a common confusion we need to clear up: starring versus watching.

[JAMIE]
Yes. People often star something and then wonder whether they subscribed to all its activity.

[ALEX]
Starring a repository is basically bookmarking or endorsing it. It helps you remember it and can help others see it is useful or interesting. Starring is not the same as asking for notifications.

[JAMIE]
Watching is the one that affects notifications.

[ALEX]
Correct. Watching controls subscription to repository activity. If you choose All Activity, you can end up with a lot of notifications very quickly.

[JAMIE]
That leads to the common mistake: accidental watching.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Maybe you clicked Watch without understanding the level, or inherited a noisy setting. If you accidentally over-subscribed, go back to the repository's Watch menu and change it to Participating and @mentions, Custom, or Ignore, depending on your needs. If the repository is no longer relevant, unwatch it or silence it.

[JAMIE]
And for this workshop, the recommended strategy is still fairly conservative.

[ALEX]
Yes. Use Participating and @mentions for most workshop repositories unless you have a specific reason to hear more.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's give dedicated screen reader tips for the notification inbox itself.

[ALEX]
For NVDA users, move through the notification list with standard browse navigation or arrow keys, listening for each item's title, repository, and reason. If single-letter inbox shortcuts are not working, make sure focus is on the notification row rather than pure browse mode text.

[JAMIE]
For JAWS?

[ALEX]
Very similar. Use heading, link, and list navigation to understand the page structure, then move item by item through the notification list. Again, if shortcuts don't work, shift into the right interaction context by focusing the notification item.

[JAMIE]
And for VoiceOver?

[ALEX]
Use VO navigation to move through the page regions and list content. When you reach notification items, listen for the repeated structure: title, repository, reason. Activate the item to open it, then return to the inbox and continue triage.

[JAMIE]
So the broad accessibility lesson is: learn the page pattern, then use your screen reader's strongest navigation style for repeated items.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Notifications are much easier once you treat the inbox as a structured list instead of a mystery page.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
There was also a note about mobile.

[ALEX]
Yes. If you use the GitHub mobile app, configure push notification preferences there intentionally. Mobile can be useful for high-priority awareness, but it can also become the fastest route to overload if every repository starts buzzing your phone.

[JAMIE]
So mobile should follow the same philosophy as email and web: urgent things on, ambient noise down.

[ALEX]
Perfect.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let's turn this into a practical challenge. Tame your inbox. Change at least one watch setting. Open your notifications inbox. Test at least two filters, such as Review requested and Assigned. Then perform one action: mute or mark done.

[JAMIE]
And if someone wants to go further, they can also visit account notification settings and revise email, web, Actions, watching, custom routing, and mobile preferences.

[ALEX]
Yes. In the bonus challenge, the checklist includes email notifications, web notifications, watching, custom routing if you use multiple emails, and GitHub Mobile push preferences if you use the app.

[JAMIE]
Then they should be able to answer three reflection questions: how will you know when someone requests your review, how will you avoid being overwhelmed by busy repositories, and what is your overall strategy for the GitHub notification inbox.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Read all, triage, or filter-first are all possible strategies, as long as they are intentional and sustainable.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
So what really counts as success here?

[ALEX]
The key learning objective is intentional notification management. If you changed at least one setting from the default and can explain why it reduces noise while keeping you informed about what matters, you completed the bonus well.

[JAMIE]
That's refreshingly human. Not perfection. Just a justified improvement.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let's close the day. Today you learned how to keep your GitHub inbox useful instead of overwhelming. You practiced setting watch levels, using filters to find important work, and taking action on notifications.

[JAMIE]
If this was your first time doing any of that, that's a substantial step. Notification skill is a real collaboration skill.

[ALEX]
It is. Productive contributors do not react to everything equally. They build habits. Check filtered notifications once or twice a day. Respond to review requests and assignments. Mute noise. Mark done when appropriate. Revisit settings when your work changes.

[JAMIE]
That sounds like the confidence check.

[ALEX]
Yes: can you find work that needs your attention, and can you prevent unimportant updates from taking over? If yes, you are building a sustainable workflow.

[JAMIE]
And your progress is not just technical. It's strategic.

[ALEX]
Exactly. You already know more than you think.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we finish, where should learners go when details change over time?

[ALEX]
The authoritative sources are GitHub Docs and the GitHub Changelog. For this topic specifically, GitHub's notifications documentation is the source of truth, especially since settings, labels, and interface details can evolve.

[JAMIE]
So learn the concepts deeply, and verify the exact current interface in the docs.

[ALEX]
That's the right habit.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Next time, you'll build on this foundation. But for now, if you can keep your inbox calm enough to notice review requests, assignments, and real collaboration signals, you've done important work today.

[JAMIE]
And maybe, for once, your notification bell won't feel like a threat.

[ALEX]
That is the dream.

# Solution Reference: Bonus D -- Notification Mastery

This shows a configured notification setup with before/after.

## Important Context: Web-First Notification Management

This bonus focuses on **GitHub's web notification inbox** as the primary way to manage notifications. Email notifications are optional and not required for this workshop. The configuration shown here demonstrates how to set up your GitHub account to manage notifications effectively whether you choose to use email or not.

**The key principle:** Use GitHub's web inbox at `github.com/notifications` as your main workflow. Enable email only if you choose to, and even then, only for high-priority items.

## Before: Default settings

With default settings, GitHub sends email notifications for:

- Every issue and PR in every repository you watch
- Every comment on any thread you have participated in
- Every CI status update

This quickly becomes overwhelming. Most people start ignoring all GitHub emails. Instead, most professional developers use the web notification inbox.

## After: Configured settings

### Notification settings (github.com/settings/notifications)

- **Participating:** Email ON, Web ON -- you want to know when someone replies to your conversations
- **Watching:** Email OFF, Web ON -- browse these when you have time, not in your inbox
- **GitHub Actions:** Email OFF for successful runs, Email ON for failed runs only

### Repository watching

- **Repositories you actively contribute to:** Watch (all activity)
- **Repositories you read occasionally:** Custom (issues and PRs only)
- **Repositories you finished with:** Unwatch

### Custom routing (if you use multiple emails)

- Route `Community-Access` organization notifications to your workshop email
- Route personal project notifications to your personal email

## Key decisions explained

- **Why email off for watching:** You can check the notification bell on github.com when you choose. Email notifications for watched repos create constant interruption for low-priority updates.
- **Why Actions failures only:** A green checkmark in the PR is enough. You only need an email when something breaks.
- **Why unwatch finished repos:** Your notification feed stays relevant to current work.

## What matters

The learning objective is intentional notification management. If you changed at least one setting from the default and can explain why that change reduces noise while keeping you informed about what matters, you completed this bonus.

## Authoritative Sources

Use these official references when you need the current source of truth for facts in this chapter.

- [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en)
- [GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/)

### Section-Level Source Map

Use this map to verify facts for each major section in this file.

- **Before: Default settings:** [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en), [GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/)
- **After: Configured settings:** [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en), [GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/)
- **Key decisions explained:** [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en), [GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/)
- **What matters:** [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en), [GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/)

# Notifications
>
> **Listen to Episode 10:** [Notifications and Mentions](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

> **Related appendices:** [Appendix T: Community and Social](appendix-t-community-and-social.md) | [Appendix U: Discussions and Gists](appendix-u-discussions-and-gists.md) | [Appendix V: GitHub Mobile](appendix-v-github-mobile.md)
> **Authoritative sources:** [GitHub Docs: About notifications](https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/managing-subscriptions-and-notifications-on-github/setting-up-notifications/about-notifications)

## Managing Your GitHub Notification Inbox

> **See also:** [Appendix V: GitHub Mobile](appendix-v-github-mobile.md) for managing notifications on your phone.

> GitHub notifications are how GitHub tells you when something needs your attention. This guide teaches you to keep the inbox useful - not overwhelming - using only your keyboard and screen reader.

## Workshop Recommendation (Chapter 10)

For this workshop, Chapter 10 is a **guided practice chapter**, not a graded automation chapter.

- **Challenge count:** 1 guided walkthrough
- **Automation check:** none - notification settings are account-level and cannot be validated by the Learning Room PR bot
- **Evidence:** structured completion comment on your assigned challenge issue
- **Pattern:** configure, filter, act

### Important Note: This Challenge Uses GitHub's Web Notification Inbox

This challenge focuses on **GitHub's web-based notification inbox** (at `github.com/notifications`), not email notifications. You do NOT need to configure email delivery, and you do NOT need to receive emails to complete this challenge.

**Why we focus on the web inbox:**

- Email delivery depends on your mail server, ISP, spam filters, and account settings—factors outside our control
- GitHub's web notification inbox is always available and works the same way for everyone
- Professional developers typically check notifications in the GitHub app or web UI rather than waiting for emails
- The skills you learn (filtering, muting, managing noise) apply whether you eventually enable email or not

**What you will do:**

- Use GitHub's web notification inbox to view and filter notifications
- Configure repository watch levels to control what notifications you receive
- Practice managing your inbox with GitHub's built-in actions (mute, mark done)

If you have already configured email notifications on your GitHub account, that is fine—but this challenge does not require or test email delivery. Focus on the web inbox workflow instead.

### Chapter 10 Challenge Set

1. **Configure notifications and practice inbox management** - set your watch level, use filters to find relevant notifications, and perform one inbox action.

### Challenge 10.1 Step-by-Step: Notification Inbox Walkthrough

**Goal:** Set up a useful notification workflow so you can keep up with reviews, mentions, and assignments without inbox overload.

**Where you are working:** the GitHub.com notifications page and your Learning Room repository settings.

**Estimated time:** 5-8 minutes.

1. Open your Learning Room repository on GitHub.com.
2. Find the **Watch** button near the top-right of the repository page (next to Star and Fork).
3. Activate the **Watch** dropdown and select **Participating and @mentions**. This means you only get notified when someone @mentions you or you are directly participating in a thread.
4. Open the notifications inbox by navigating to `https://github.com/notifications` (or activate the bell icon in the GitHub header).
5. In the notification filters, activate the **Review requested** filter. This shows only notifications where someone has asked you to review their PR.
6. Clear that filter and activate the **Assigned** filter. This shows notifications for issues and PRs assigned to you.
7. Open one notification by activating its title link. Read it briefly, then navigate back to the inbox.
8. Perform one inbox action on a non-critical notification thread:
   - Press `M` to **mute** the thread (you will not receive future updates), or

## What Generates a Notification?

GitHub sends you a notification when:

| Event | You are notified if... |
| -------  | ------------------------  |
| Someone @mentions you | `@your-username` appears in any issue, PR, or discussion |
| A PR is assigned to you for review | You are added as a reviewer |
| An issue or PR is assigned to you | You are assigned |
| There is activity on a thread you are subscribed to | You commented, were mentioned, or chose to subscribe |
| A CI check fails on your PR | Actions sends a failure notification |
| A release is published | You are watching the repo for all activity |

## Notification Subscription Levels

For each repository, you choose how many notifications to receive:

| Level | What You Receive |
| -------  | -----------------  |
| **Participating and @mentions** | Only notifications where you participated (commented, were assigned, @mentioned). Recommended for most repos. |
| **All Activity** | Every issue opened, every comment, every PR. Only use this for your own repos or very active contribution. |
| **Ignore** | No notifications from this repo at all. |
| **Custom** | Fine-grained control: issues only, PRs only, releases, etc. |

## Starring vs. Watching - What Is the Difference?

New contributors often confuse these two. They appear next to each other on every repository page and do completely different things.

### Starring a Repository

| Feature | Description |
| ---  | ---  |
| **What it does** | Bookmarks the repository to your Stars list at `github.com/stars` |
| **Notifications** | **None.** Starring never sends you any notifications |
| **Visibility** | Public - anyone can see what you've starred on your profile |
| **Use case** | "I want to save this for later" or "I want to show appreciation" |
| **Keyboard path** | On any repo page: `B` to navigate buttons → find "Star" button → Enter |

Starring is GitHub's equivalent of a bookmark + public endorsement. The star count on a repository is a community signal of popularity. Many maintainers watch their star count as a rough measure of interest.

### Watching a Repository

| Feature | Description |
| ---  | ---  |
| **What it does** | Subscribes you to notifications from that repository |
| **Notifications** | Sends notifications based on your chosen level (see below) |
| **Visibility** | Private - other users cannot see what you're watching |
| **Use case** | "I need to stay informed about activity in this repo" |
| **Keyboard path** | `B` → find "Watch" button → Enter → ↑/↓ to pick a level → Enter |

### Common Mistake: Accidental Watching

When you comment on an issue or PR in a repository, GitHub **automatically subscribes you** to that thread - but not the whole repository. However, if you once click "Watch" on a busy repository (say, a popular open source project), you will receive a notification for every issue opened and every comment posted - potentially hundreds per day.

#### How to silence a repository you accidentally over-subscribed to

```text
Step 1: Navigate to the repository
Step 2: B → Find "Unwatch" button → Enter
Step 3: Select "Participating and @mentions"
Step 4: Enter to confirm
```

This immediately reduces notifications from that repository to only threads you personally participated in.

### Recommended Watching Strategy for This Workshop

| Repository | Recommended Watch Level |
| ---  | ---  |
| `community-access/accessibility-agents` | **Participating and @mentions** - you contribute there, you only need to hear back when someone replies to you |
| Your own fork | **All Activity** - this is your fork; know everything |
| Very busy popular repos | **Ignore** or **Participating** - do not watch for All Activity |
| Repos you're evaluating | **Star only** - save without subscribing |

3. **Try a GitHub Skills course.** [GitHub Skills](https://skills.github.com/) offers free, self-paced courses that run inside real repositories. "Introduction to GitHub" is a good one if you want to reinforce what you learned today. See [Appendix Z](appendix-z-github-skills.md) for the full list of recommended courses.

> **Screen reader tip:** GitHub Skills courses use bot-driven feedback inside pull requests. The interaction model is similar to the Learning Room -- you push a change, a bot reviews it, and you get instructions for the next step. If you completed today's challenges, you already know the workflow.

### You Already Know More Than You Think

Think about where you started this morning. You may not have known what a repository was, or how to navigate one with a keyboard, or what happens when two people edit the same file. Now you do. You have created real issues, opened real pull requests, resolved real conflicts, and configured your own notification workflow -- all in a live, shared codebase.

Day 2 builds on every one of those skills. Nothing gets thrown away. Everything you did today is the foundation for everything that comes next.

> **End of Day 1:** Congratulations. You have completed **Challenge 9: Merge Day** and finished the browser-based foundation. [Return to the Course Guide](course-guide.md) to prepare for Day 2.

voiceRules.voiceExemplar:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're working with one of those GitHub features that quietly makes open source collaboration much easier: issue templates.

[JAMIE]
And this is a great one for people who have ever opened a blank issue form and thought, what exactly am I supposed to put here?

[ALEX]
Exactly. An issue template turns that blank box into a guided experience. Instead of guessing what maintainers need, contributors get prompts, structure, and clear required fields. That reduces back-and-forth, improves quality, and helps teams act on issues faster.

[JAMIE]
So this is not just about formatting. It's about making contributions clearer and more usable.

[ALEX]
Yes, and especially in accessibility work. If someone is reporting an accessibility barrier, a vague report can be hard to reproduce. A thoughtful template can ask where the problem occurred, what assistive technology was involved, what the expected behavior was, and how severe the barrier is.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we get into the design challenge, what should learners already have in place?

[ALEX]
A few practical things. First, you should already know how to work with GitHub issues at a basic level. Second, you need a repository where you can create or edit files, usually your fork or your own repo. Third, it really helps to use an editor with YAML syntax highlighting, such as VS Code.

[JAMIE]
And some things are recommended but not strictly required, right?

[ALEX]
Right. Familiarity with GitHub Copilot can help if you want to generate variations, but it's optional. Basic terminal comfort is useful, though you can also use the GitHub web editor or github.dev. And if you already filled out the workshop registration template earlier in this course, that template becomes a learning example now.

[JAMIE]
I like that. You've already used a professional issue template, so now you reverse-engineer it.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Also, there's an administrative note here: this chapter is meant to prepare you for a later workflow using a template-building agent. The advice is to complete the manual template chapter first, then use the automation later.

[JAMIE]
And time-wise?

[ALEX]
Plan roughly two to two and a half hours if you do the exercises and some YAML troubleshooting.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
The learning pattern for this challenge is analyze, remix, create, and test.

[JAMIE]
That feels approachable. First understand an existing template, then adapt one, then optionally build another version from scratch, then verify it works.

[ALEX]
That's the idea. The workshop recommendation frames Challenge 14 as design-focused rather than automation-focused. You're producing evidence of understanding, often as an issue comment or a pull request, rather than trying to satisfy a complicated code runtime.

[JAMIE]
Though there is still one small autograded requirement in the challenge template itself.

[ALEX]
Yes. For the assigned challenge issue, the autograder checks that a YAML file exists in the repository
